In (b), the sample size is replaced by the context (train) set size (see Section 5). MAE-Hinge. We use absolute error for event times and a one-sided hinge error for censored times: MAEHinge = 1 n n X i=1  δi|ti −ˆti| + (1 −δi) max(0, ti −ˆti)  , where δi indicates an observed event and ˆti is the predicted median survival time. For censored individuals, only predictions earlier than the censoring time are penalized. KM-Calibration. We assess marginal calibration with the normalized integrated squared error, in [0, 1], between the average predicted survival curve 1 Ntest P i bS(t | xi) and the Kaplan–Meier curve of the test set (Chapfuwa et al., 2020). 6.2 BASELINES: FROM COX TO FOUNDATION MODELS All models are described in more detail in Appendix B.1, we refer to Table 3 for a synthetic overview. Shallow models. We include Cox model (Cox, 1972) and KM estimator (Kaplan and Meier, 1958) as baselines. The latter does not use covariates, and hence any model is expected to outperform it. Deep Networks. We include five deep networks tailored for survival analysis (Lee et al., 2018; Katzman et al., 2018; Nagpal et al., 2021; Rindt et al., 2022; Kirpichenko et al., 2026). These models are fitted on each dataset and use various modeling techniques (from Bayesian prior to a MLP that predicts the survival function at different times). Tree-Based Models. Following the seminal work of Ishwaran et al. (2008) on random survival forests (RSF) and Grinsztajn et al. (2022), a body of work has adapted tree-based methods to survival analysis. On top of RSF, we evaluate SurvivalBoost (Alberge et al., 2024) and alternative gradient- boosted tree-based methods implemented in sksurv (P¨olsterl, 2020). Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs). We include four open-weight tabular foundation models in our benchmark: SurvPFN (B¨ohm et al., 2026), SurvivalPFN (Qi et al., 2026), Survival-IC (SIC) (Seletkov et al., 2026) and TFM4Survival (Kim et al., 2026). 6.3 DATASETS AND HOLD-OUT PROTOCOL In total, we consider 103 datasets with varying properties, see Figure 3. The datasets are partitioned into 40 development datasets used during model development and 63 held-out datasets at random. For development, we source 2 PyCox (Kvamme et al., 2019), 25 SurvSet (Drysdale, 2022), one from a challenge and 12 cBioPortal (Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013; De Bruijn et al., 2023) datasets. For held-out datasets, we use 6 from Pycox, 39 from SurvSet and 18 datasets from cBioPortal. Protocol. All design choices of SurvICL (prior, target, and checkpoint) were made using the 40 development datasets; the 63 held-out datasets were kept for the final evaluation. We evaluated each method over ten event-stratified 80/20 train–test splits (test sets capped at 4,096 observations). 7
